style: emoji-heavy texting, fragments, no capitals; thinks the problem is the park until the fourth entry

situations.name: Going to the park playground (the real trigger is off-leash dogs there)
situations.feared_outcome: A dog will run at me and bite my face

behaviors.text: Says his legs hurt or he is tired so they go home instead of to the park
Climbs up mom and wants to be carried whenever a dog is in sight
Asks over and over whether there will be dogs there before going

accommodations.text: Mom takes him to the indoor trampoline park instead of the park
Mom tells him she checked and there are no dogs, or that the dog is on a leash

situations.name: Visiting Grandpa's house (Grandpa has a big dog, Gus)

behaviors.text: Only gets out of the car and goes inside once Gus is shut in the backyard
Runs back out to the car when Gus barks at the back door

accommodations.text: Mom texts Grandpa from the driveway to shut Gus out back (or in the garage) before Teddy comes in

situations.name: Walking past the neighbor's fenced yard with a barking dog
situations.feared_outcome: The dog will jump over the fence

behaviors.text: Pulls mom across the street so they don't pass the fence

accommodations.text: Mom crosses the street with him

turns.text: Hi Teddy, hi Mom. Come on in. Teddy, grab whichever seat you like. So this is our third time meeting, and I like to start by looking back at the week. Mom, I can see you've been putting a lot into the log. What stood out to you?

The big thing is I finally figured out it's not the park. For a couple of weeks I thought he just didn't like the playground anymore, or he was worn out after school. Then on Saturday a dog got loose near the swings, a big yellow lab, and he completely lost it. He climbed up me. Afterwards in the car he told me the dog was going to bite his face.
That is a really useful thing to have noticed. Teddy, is that right? Is it the dogs at the park that feel scary?
Yeah. Dogs can just run at you and jump on you.
They can run at you and jump on you. What do you think would happen if a dog jumped on you?
It would bite me in the face. That's what happened to Owen's cousin.
There's a boy in his class whose cousin got bitten, I think last summer. I don't know the details. He's brought it up a few times now, at bedtime mostly.

Okay. So you heard a story about somebody getting bitten, and now when you see a dog your body sets off an alarm. That makes a lot of sense, Teddy. Your brain is trying to keep you safe. What we do here is help your brain learn which dogs are actually okay. Do you remember the fear thermometer? Zero to ten?
Ten is the worst you could ever feel.
Ten is the worst, that's right. So if you're at the park and there's a dog walking on a leash, way over on the other side, by the parking lot, where are you on the thermometer?
Seven.
Seven. Thank you for telling me. And if the dog was off the leash and running around?
Ten. Like a hundred.
On Saturday when the lab got loose he told me nine. Then in the car he said a hundred, so, that matches.

That helps. Mom, I want to ask about something I saw in the log. A few times Teddy asks, are there dogs, are there dogs, before you even leave the house. And one day you told him you'd checked and there weren't any. Tell me what's going on for you in that moment.

Honestly, I say whatever gets us out the door. If I say I don't know, he won't put his shoes on. That day I told him there were no dogs, and then there was one right by the slide, and I felt terrible. I wrote it down because I figured you'd want to know.

I'm glad you wrote it down, and it is a completely normal thing for a parent to do. Here is what tends to happen, though. When he asks and you answer, he feels better for a minute. Then the worry comes back and he needs to ask again. The asking starts doing the job that he could be learning to do himself. And when the answer turns out to be wrong, like Tuesday, the next promise counts for less. So I want to help you answer differently, not stop caring.
So what do I actually say? Because he will ask twenty times.

You answer once, kindly, and then you name the worry. Something like, there might be dogs, and I know you can handle it, and I'll be right there. After that, if he asks again, you can say, that's the worry asking, and we already answered it. Then talk about something else. It will feel mean the first few times. It isn't.
I don't want there to be dogs.

I know you don't. We're not going to make you go pet a big dog. We're going to do small steps, and you get to help pick them. Okay? Can I ask Mom about Grandpa's house first, and then we'll pick a step together?
Okay.
Mom, Grandpa's house came up twice in the log.

Right. My dad has a big dog named Gus. He's a sweetheart, honestly, an old shepherd mix, but he's huge. Teddy won't unbuckle until I've texted my dad to put Gus in the backyard. Once Gus is out, he comes in and he's totally fine, he builds Legos with my dad for hours. But last Thursday Gus barked at the sliding door, and Teddy bolted straight out to the car. I sat out there with him for, I don't know, twenty minutes, while my dad moved Gus to the garage.
So he goes in, but only once Gus is put away, and when Gus barked he left. Those are two different things and both are useful to know. Teddy, what's Gus like?
He's really big. He's nice to Grandpa. But he barks super loud at the door.
Has Gus ever bitten anybody?
No. But he could.
He could. That's what the worry says. Mom, did you get a number from him at Grandpa's, on the thermometer?
No, I didn't think to ask. I was just trying to get him back inside.

That's fine. Next time you're there, see if he'll give you one, and write it down. It'll help us decide where Gus goes on his ladder. I want to leave Grandpa's for next week, though. I think it's too big to start with. There was also the dog behind the fence on the way to school?
Oh, that was just once. He pulled me across the street. I didn't push it.

Okay, we'll come back to that one too. So, Teddy, here is my idea for a first step, and you tell me what you think. At home, you and Mom watch a short video of puppies. Just a few minutes. You hold the tablet, so you're in charge of it. What number would that be?
Puppy videos are like a two. Maybe a one if they're really small.

Okay, that sounds like a good warm up. Then the real step: once this week at the park, you and Mom stand by the fence near the parking lot, and watch a dog walk by on a leash. You stay standing on your own feet, next to Mom, and you count to twenty slowly. Mom doesn't pick you up. What number is that?
Five. Maybe six.
Five or six. That's a good number for a brave step. It should feel a bit hard, but nowhere near a ten. Can you try it?
Only if it's a small dog.
We can't pick the dog, but if it's a big one you can stand farther back. Mom, how does that sound?
Doable. The not picking him up is going to be the hard part for me.

I know. That's your step for the week. And with the asking, answer once and then name the worry, like we talked about. Write down what happened, and what number he gives you. Puppy videos most days, the park step once, and no checking for dogs ahead of time. Does that sound like the plan?
Yes. Puppy videos, the fence thing once, and I stop doing the dog patrol.
Can I be the one who picks the videos?
You absolutely can pick the videos. Good work today, Teddy. I'll see you both next week.
